text.p: The following is a direct contribution from commodity statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.
COFFEE - COFFEE: World market for March 21, 1997

Robusta futures in London ended with pared gains after a relatively quiet session which saw some light buying interest in the back months. By the close, May stood $8 higher at $1,663 per tonne after ranging between $1,655 and $1,670.

Trade sources said the market was trying to digest news of a hike in arabica exports announced by the Association of Coffee Producing Countries. While the supply tightness might loosen up in the short term following the move by the ACPC, the long term supply concerns linger.
Arabica futures in New York ended mixed, with the nearbys pulling back amid news that more arabica coffee would be finding its way to the market, dealers said.

Most active May fell 3.40 cents/lb on the day to 165.75 cents/lb, after ranging between 171.20 and 165.50. Second month July finished 1.65 cents/lb lower at 155.55 cents/lb, while the back months closed down 0.80 to up 2.05 cents.

The ACPC decision to release an additional 200,000 bags of washed arabica coffee triggered a commission house sell off, traders said. On the charts, May near term support was seen at 165.50 cents, while resistant was pegged at 172.00 cents, it was said.

COLOMBIA - Colombia lowered its internal coffee price by 5.12 per cent on March 21, setting it at 363,750 pesos per 125-kg load, the National Coffee Growers' Federation said. The price had been raised 6 times since January 31, as the federation moved to bring internal price closer into line with world prices. The new price was based on average Colombian coffee prices in New York over the past week, it was added.

COLOMBIA - Colombia's main truckers' association voted on March 22 to start an indefinite, nationwide strike on April 20 and vowed to bring all road freight to a standstill. The stoppage was called to protest transport companies' failure to fulfill terms of a deal hammered out to end a crippling 11-day strike by truckers in October 1996.

The stoppage could wreak havoc with all sectors of the industry, including the key coffee sector, which by April 20 will be in the middle of the so-called Mitaca harvest, which provides about 40 per cent of annual coffee production. The main harvest is in late October. Last October's strike delayed the exports of more than 305,000 60-kg bags and already private exporters have said a new transport strike will be disastrous.
BRAZIL - The Brazilian government will auction a total of 326,188 60-kg bags of coffee from government stocks on April 2. In March the government auctioned a total of 256,990 bags.

MEXICO - Mexico exported 883,725 60-kg bags of coffee in February 1997 compared to 744,586 bags shipped in the same month in 1996, the Mexican Coffee Council said. The council, the government umbrella organization covering the entire coffee sector, said the export figure represented a 18.7 per cent rise from February 1996. The new figure is an all-time monthly record for exports from Mexico. In the first five months of the 1996/97 cycle the council said Mexico exported 2.634 mn bags of coffee compared to 2.310 mn bags in the same period in 1995/96.

UNITED STATES - According to Complete Coffee Coverage, US green coffee roastings for the week ended March 15 totalled approximately 325,000 60-kg bags, up from 305,000 the previous week and compared with 325,000 bags in the corresponding period one year ago. Cumulative roastings so far totalled 3.945 mn 60-kg bags versus 3.805 mn bags in the same year ago period.
